report_text:
# FSMA 204 action brief for Lee’s Market
**To:** Emily Patel, Regulatory Affairs Manager  
**Case reference date:** 27 August 2025  
**Regulatory status note checked:** 20 November 2026

## Recommendation
Use FSMA 204 as a lot-level operating discipline across covered suppliers, distribution, stores, fresh-food preparation, and e-commerce. Start with a product-and-facility scope map, capture lot data at receiving, retain lot links through any covered transformation or business-to-business shipment, and prove retrieval through mock trace exercises. That capability can support faster, narrower holds and more accurate customer notices. Lee’s should communicate only what its lot records verify; the internal records do not establish a food-safety-specific customer-trust gain or a completed traceability test. [1–4, 7–9]

## What likely applies
The rule applies to foods on FDA’s Food Traceability List (FTL) and the critical tracking events (CTEs) a covered person performs, subject to exemptions. The likely Lee’s assortment to screen first includes specified leafy greens, herbs, cucumbers, peppers, tomatoes, melons, tropical tree fruits, sprouts and fresh-cut produce; listed seafood categories; shell eggs; non-hard cheeses; nut butters; and certain ready-to-eat deli salads. Do not treat all produce or seafood as covered: qualify the exact item, species, and form. Foods containing an FTL ingredient are covered only under the rule’s ingredient/form conditions; meat salads are excluded from the FTL deli-salad category. Meat and poultry are not generally standalone FTL categories, and bakery and other prepared foods are not automatically covered. Confirm ingredients, food state, preparation steps, and regulatory jurisdiction SKU by SKU. [1–3, 5]

For covered receiving events, configure capture of the product description, quantity and unit, receipt date and location, traceability lot code (TLC), TLC source, immediate previous source, and reference-document type/number. Covered entities retain records for two years and must provide them to FDA within 24 hours or another reasonable time agreed with FDA; FDA can also request an electronic sortable spreadsheet. Use existing ERP/WMS/POS tools if they reliably link and retrieve the required records; the rule does not require a particular commercial platform. [1, 3, 4]

Lee’s U.S. and Canadian footprint makes a facility and destination map important: confirm which legal entities and facilities handle FTL foods for U.S. consumption, what activities they perform, and which exemptions actually apply. Do not infer a retailer exemption from chain-wide revenue. Counsel should resolve borderline SKU, ingredient, transformation, and facility questions before the scope is approved. [1–3, 5]

## Lee’s readiness and priorities
Internal records say the inventory system tracked approximately 250 high-risk food products, nearly 30% of inventory, as of Q3 2024, while additional controls and data capture were still being implemented. A 15 July 2025 email reports an 85% compliance rate among high-risk food suppliers, but the underlying report, denominator, and definition were not retrieved. Treat both as leads for validation, not proof of FSMA 204 readiness. [7, 8]

A 2023 simulated recall identified communication-protocol and supply-chain responsiveness issues; the company said it strengthened notification procedures and planned regular crisis-team training. The records do not provide a measured trace time or a later retest. An April 2024 training email reported 90% completion and an average of 12 training hours, but explicitly said that training was not FSMA 204-specific. [7, 9]

## 30/60/90-day implementation
**Days 0–30 — Scope and baseline.** Create one controlled matrix by SKU, ingredient/form, supplier, facility, destination, and CTE. Classify FTL items and flag store/DC receiving, store transfers, direct-to-consumer orders, and activities that may be transformation (such as cutting, repacking, seafood or deli preparation). Record legal decisions and exemptions with counsel. Baseline supplier data completeness, store receiving practices, and present traceback time. [1–3, 5]

**Days 31–60 — Supplier and store workflows.** Issue a common supplier data specification for exact product description (including species/form where relevant), TLC, TLC source, immediate previous source, quantity/unit, and usable reference documents. Test imported items, supplier substitutions, weight-based receipts, and supplier lot-code formats. At receiving, scan or record the lot at case level, match product and quantity to the invoice/ASN, and resolve missing or conflicting data before disposition. Preserve the received TLC through inventory and subsequent use. For covered inter-site or business-to-business shipments, record the shipping KDEs, including ship-from and recipient locations, date, product/quantity, TLC, and reference document, and transmit required information to the recipient. [1, 3, 4, 10, 11]

For online picking and delivery, retain an internal connection between inventory lots and affected order lines, including substitutions, so Lee’s can identify relevant customers during a recall. FDA provides a limited direct-to-consumer shipping-record exception for retail food establishments; it does not remove receiving or transformation duties and should not be extended to business-to-business transfers without checking the facts. Preserve the order-to-lot link as an operational recall control even where a shipping KDE exception applies. [1, 3, 11]

For any process that qualifies as transformation, configure records to link every input TLC and quantity to the output product/TLC and quantity, with the transformation date, location, and reference document. Have food-safety and legal owners review cutting, repacking, mixing, commingling, seafood preparation, recipe changes, and deli preparation against FDA definitions rather than assuming the result. [1, 3, 10]

**Days 61–90 — Pilot and prove.** Pilot at a distribution center and representative stores covering produce, seafood, imported and weight-based items, prepared-food workflows, and online orders. Run a backward trace from a customer order or store lot to supplier records and a forward trace from a supplier lot to all affected stores, transformed batches, business recipients, inventory, and orders. Measure missing KDEs, lot/quantity reconciliation, time to place a hold, affected-order accuracy, customer-notice preparation time, and whether records can be assembled within FDA’s 24-hour access window. Train receivers, produce/seafood/deli teams, buyers, and recall staff on their specific steps; fix gaps before wider rollout. Test likely failure modes—including inconsistent lot formats, lost case-to-unit links, species or language mismatches, repacking/commingling, recipe changes, cross-store transfers, and online substitutions. These are test scenarios, not confirmed Lee’s system defects. [1, 3, 7, 9–11]

## Measures and customer communication
Track: (1) candidate SKUs reviewed and FTL decisions with a documented rationale/owner; (2) covered receipts complete and matched for required KDEs; (3) supplier data completeness and exception-resolution time; (4) transformed batches with input-to-output links and quantity reconciliation; (5) lots traceable across site transfers; (6) mock-recall time to identify stock/orders, hold product, and prepare a factual notice; (7) employee training completion by job; and (8) customer notice accuracy and timeliness. Set tighter internal trace targets after the pilot establishes a baseline. Add a food-safety confidence question to customer research rather than using general CRM engagement as a proxy. [1, 3, 7–11]

When a trace identifies an issue, use verified lot and order data to hold only the implicated stock where supported, notify the right locations and customers, and give clear instructions. Do not market FSMA 204 compliance as a guarantee that food is risk-free. The rule’s traceability purpose supports faster identification and removal of potentially contaminated food, while Lee’s internal records report no food-safety-specific trust measure. [1, 7]

## Timing
As of the case date, the original compliance date was 20 January 2026. FDA had announced an intention to extend it in March 2025 and, on 6 August 2025, proposed a 30-month extension to 20 July 2028; on 27 August 2025 that was a proposal, not a finalized amendment. FDA’s rule page checked on 20 November 2026 still describes the extension as proposed and reports a subsequent Congressional direction that FDA not enforce before 20 July 2028. Maintain the implementation plan and have counsel verify the operative date and enforcement position before relying on any delay. [1, 5, 6]

[3] FDA, “Frequently Asked Questions: FSMA Food Traceability Rule” — https://www.fda.gov/food/food-safety-modernization-act-fsma/frequently-asked-questions-fsma-food-traceability-rule

report_insights.claim: FSMA 204 scope depends on FTL foods and the CTEs performed; Lee’s should classify SKUs, ingredients, food state, activities, facilities, and U.S. destinations before declaring coverage.
citations: FDA, FSMA Food Traceability Rule FAQs — https://www.fda.gov/food/food-safety-modernization-act-fsma/frequently-asked-questions-fsma-food-traceability-rule

report_insights.claim: Coverage cannot be inferred from broad departments: Lee’s must resolve produce item/form, seafood species/form, FTL ingredient conditions, and deli-salad type; meat and poultry are not generally standalone FTL categories, and meat salads are excluded from the FTL deli-salad category.

report_insights.claim: Lee’s internal baseline includes approximately 250 high-risk food products tracked in Q3 2024 and a reported 85% high-risk-supplier compliance rate in July 2025, but the available records do not define the latter metric or prove FSMA 204 traceability completeness.

Store receiving, transformations, B2B shipments, and e-commerce should be mapped separately; a limited direct-to-consumer shipping exception should not be treated as a waiver for other events, and order-to-lot links are a useful recall control.

report_insights.claim: Lot-level traceability can support accurate, targeted recall and customer updates, but Lee’s has no documented food-safety-specific trust measure in the retrieved internal records; survey it directly and avoid unsupported assurance claims.

report_insights.claim: Traceability workflows should preserve lot identity through transformation and business-to-business movement, including input/output lot and quantity links, shipment KDEs, and order-to-lot links for voluntary recall response; test likely failure modes without assuming they are present at Lee’s.
